title: Quantum query complexity versus bounded approximate degree
formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the extremal function \[M(n,d)=\max\bigl\{Q(f):\varnothing\ne D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ f:D\to\{0,1\},\ \operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\le d\bigr\}\] for all integers \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le d\le n\). The bounded approximate degree \(\operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\) is the least total degree of a real polynomial \(p\) satisfying \[|p(x)-f(x)|\le1/3\quad(x\in D),\qquad 0\le p(x)\le1\quad(x\in\{0,1\}^n).\] The query measure \(Q\) has worst-case error at most \(1/3\). This makes the source's largest-gap question a two-parameter extremal query bound. The source's additional question of whether an exponential gap exists was answered affirmatively in 2023.
why: Bounded approximate degree is the main numerical object behind the polynomial method for quantum query lower bounds. Determining its worst possible discrepancy from actual quantum query complexity would quantify how much algorithmic difficulty this method can miss under promises.
status_note: The exponential-separation part of the 2021 question was resolved by Ambainis and Belovs at CCC 2023. The card retains the broader maximum-gap target as the explicit extremal curve M(n,d). The source, published separation and 2024 follow-up were checked on 2026-09-14; their checked theorems do not determine this curve, and a bounded later-work search found no complete characterization.

progress.text: Aaronson asks for the largest bounded-degree-versus-quantum-query gap for partial Boolean functions and whether it can be exponential.
Ambainis and Belovs prove an exponential separation, with full-cube boundedness retained after encoding the alphabet into Boolean bits.
Ben-David and Kundu reprove the partial-function exponential separation and establish related separations for stronger measures and total search problems.

importance.reason: Relates quantum query algorithms to polynomial approximation, connecting two core tools for quantum upper and lower bounds.

sentences: The question compares quantum query complexity with polynomials that approximate a promised Boolean function.
The polynomial must remain between zero and one even on inputs outside the promise.
The target is the largest quantum query complexity possible at each input length and bounded-degree budget.
A 2023 theorem already proves that the gap can be exponential, so that subquestion is no longer open.
The remaining task is to determine the full extremal bound up to universal multiplicative constants.

definitions:
A partial Boolean function has a nonempty promise domain \(D\) of valid inputs, with one prescribed output bit for each valid input. An algorithm knows the function and promise but receives the actual input only through its bit oracle. Correctness is required on \(D\). Its fixed query budget applies on every input, including inputs outside the promise, where the output bit may be arbitrary.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

A real polynomial is a finite linear combination of monomials in \(n\) real variables; its total degree is the largest sum of variable exponents in a monomial with nonzero coefficient. Multilinear polynomials suffice because \(x_i^j=x_i\) on Boolean inputs for \(j\ge1\). Their real coefficients have no bit-length or computability restriction. Boundedness is imposed only on the entire Boolean cube, not on all of \(\mathbb R^n\), and includes inputs outside the promise. Every partial Boolean function has a bounded exact representing polynomial of degree at most \(n\): extend its values to a total Boolean function and interpolate.

There are finitely many partial Boolean functions on a fixed cube, so the displayed maximum is over a finite set. It is nonempty and satisfies \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain, using a single input-bit function for the lower bound and reading all bits for the upper bound. The parameter \(n\) counts individual Boolean oracle bits. A symbol from a larger alphabet is not available in one query. Neither the promise nor the polynomial is supplied as an additional input-dependent oracle.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified positive function \(H(n,d)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(cH(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le CH(n,d)\) throughout the stated integer domain. The answer must identify the asymptotic dependence on \(n,d\), not merely rename the defining optimization over functions or algorithms. Both a universal upper bound and matching worst-case examples are required. Exponential separation alone is already known and does not settle this full extremal target.

context_blocks.text: A \(T\)-query quantum algorithm has an acceptance probability that is a polynomial of degree at most \(2T\), bounded between zero and one on every Boolean input. Hence bounded approximate degree is always at most twice quantum query complexity. The question asks how far the converse can fail.

The promise does not remove the full-cube boundedness condition. Omitting that condition changes the measure and permits simple examples with artificially low degree. For total Boolean functions the two measures are polynomially related, but promises permit much larger separations.

Ambainis and Belovs give Boolean promise functions on \(n\) bits with bounded exact polynomial degree \(O(\log n)\) and quantum query complexity at least \(n^{1/3}\) up to logarithmic losses along their family. Bounded exact degree also upper-bounds bounded approximate degree, so this answers the exponential-gap subquestion.

The 2024 paper reproves such a partial-function separation through total search problems and strengthens the polynomial measure in additional results. These results establish large gaps, but the checked theorems do not determine the full extremal dependence on the input length and degree budget.
